text.title: Terraform (Advanced) Core Rules
text.summary: 22 testable rules + 2 routing conclusions (run-the-checklist, skip-this-methodology) grounding the terraform methodology. Directory layout patterns, file naming conventions, workspace strategies, and their isolation trade-offs. Pipeline stages, saved plan rule, security scanning, OIDC authentication, and Atlantis configuration. State architecture, module quality, CI/CD pipeline, security hardening, and production deployment checklists. The checklists are the ck-* rules. Each rule pairs a binary check + sourced rationale.

rule.statement: Apply terraform to a single instance of the triggering activity. Never batch multiple unrelated decisions through one pass.
rule.rationale: Batching turns a 1-decision artefact into a debate club. Each instance gets its own record so the rationale is traceable.

rule.statement: Every input field has a declared type and source. Free-form prose without a source citation is rejected.
rule.rationale: Untyped inputs let LLMs hallucinate plausible-but-wrong values. Typed + sourced inputs make the output falsifiable.

rule.statement: The output names a single accountable owner (handle, email, or org role). No 'team' or 'we' as owner.
rule.rationale: Plural ownership = no ownership. Future readers need a named human to chase when the artefact is stale.

rule.statement: Output carries semver-style version and last_reviewed date. Stale records (>90 days, no review) must be flagged on read.
rule.rationale: Methodology outputs decay; treating them as immutable is a defect. Versioning + review-by-date forces refresh cadence.

rule.statement: Every decision in the output cites the input artefact(s) that justified it. Untraceable decisions are rejected.
rule.rationale: Without traceability, the artefact becomes opinion. Citations make the output reviewable by a future operator with no context.

rule.statement: Organize Terraform projects as environments/dev|staging|prod (each with its own backend) plus modules/ for reusable components and global/ for account-wide resources (IAM, DNS).
rule.rationale: Environment directories with separate backends provide full blast-radius isolation — a destroy in dev cannot affect prod state. Shared backend workspaces do not provide this isolation.

rule.statement: Within each environment directory, further split by component: networking/, compute/, database/. Each component directory has its own backend key and state file.
rule.rationale: Monolithic per-environment state files mean a change to a single security group requires locking all compute and database resources. Component separation limits apply scope.

rule.statement: Use directory-per-environment over CLI workspaces for production systems; use workspaces only for lightweight variations of the same infrastructure (e.g., feature branch ephemeral environments).
rule.rationale: Workspaces share backend configuration and provider credentials. A misconfigured workspace apply can target the wrong environment. Directory isolation uses separate backend keys making cross-env accidents structurally impossible.

rule.statement: Use the standard file set: versions.tf (version constraints), providers.tf (provider config), main.tf (primary resources), variables.tf, outputs.tf, locals.tf, data.tf, backend.tf.
rule.rationale: Consistent file layout allows any team member to navigate an unfamiliar module. main.tf is the first place engineers look for resource definitions.

rule.statement: Modules must follow single responsibility — one logical component per module; no hardcoded values; parameterize everything via variables with sensible defaults; version modules with semantic versioning tags.
rule.rationale: Single-responsibility modules are reusable without modification. Hardcoded values (AMI IDs, CIDR blocks, account IDs) make modules non-portable across environments and regions.

rule.statement: Run the full pipeline in order: terraform fmt -check, terraform validate, tflint, tfsec/checkov, terraform plan -out=tfplan, human review, terraform apply tfplan.
rule.rationale: Each stage catches a different class of error: fmt catches style, validate catches syntax, tflint catches provider-specific issues, tfsec catches security misconfigurations, and the saved plan ensures apply matches reviewed output.

rule.statement: Always save the plan to a file with -out=tfplan and apply that exact file; never re-run terraform plan between plan and apply in CI.
rule.rationale: Re-planning between review and apply allows infrastructure to change state, meaning the applied plan differs from the reviewed plan. This is a common cause of production incidents in automated pipelines.

rule.statement: Run tfsec and checkov on every pull request; fail the pipeline on any CRITICAL or HIGH severity finding without an approved exception; run Infracost to surface cost impact on PRs.
rule.rationale: Security scanners catch default-insecure configurations (unencrypted S3, public RDS, wildcard IAM) before they reach production. Cost estimation prevents unexpected bill increases from infrastructure changes.

rule.statement: Use OIDC-based authentication for GitHub Actions and GitLab CI to assume cloud provider roles; never store static access keys as CI secrets.
rule.rationale: OIDC tokens are short-lived (15 minutes), scoped to the specific workflow run, and automatically expire. Static access keys are frequently leaked in CI logs, artifacts, or public repositories.

rule.statement: Configure Atlantis with per-project autoplan and apply_requirements: approved, mergeable; use Atlantis for teams that prefer plan-in-PR workflow over separate CI apply stages.
rule.rationale: Atlantis runs plan automatically on PR creation and posts output as a comment. apply_requirements: approved ensures at least one human review before any apply executes.

rule.statement: Verify: separate state files per environment AND per component; remote backend with locking and encryption; .terraform.lock.hcl committed; no state files in git; provider versions pinned.
rule.rationale: These five checks together eliminate the most common Terraform production incidents: state corruption, credential leaks, provider version drift, and blast radius from monolithic state.

rule.statement: Confirm blast-radius isolation: a destroy in one environment's state cannot affect another environment; component-level states minimize resources affected per apply.
rule.rationale: Without isolation, terraform destroy on the networking state of prod takes down the entire production network. Component isolation limits each operation's scope.

rule.statement: Verify pipeline has all stages: fmt -check, validate, tflint, tfsec/checkov, plan -out=tfplan, required human approval for prod, apply tfplan (not re-plan), post-apply health checks.
rule.rationale: Each missing stage is a class of error that reaches production without detection. The saved-plan requirement is the most commonly missing critical control.

rule.statement: Confirm: OIDC authentication (no static keys), TF_IN_AUTOMATION=true, plan artifact stored for audit, apply output logged, Dependabot/Renovate for controlled provider/module updates.
rule.rationale: Static keys are a credential leak risk. Plan artifacts provide the audit trail for change management. Automated dependency updates prevent security vulnerabilities from accumulating.

rule.statement: Verify: no hardcoded secrets in .tf files, all sensitive variables marked sensitive = true, all storage resources have encryption enabled, no 0.0.0.0/0 security group rules without justification, IAM follows least privilege.
rule.rationale: Static analysis (tfsec/checkov) catches the common cases, but manual review is needed for business-logic-specific IAM policies that scanners cannot evaluate.

rule.statement: Before prod apply: review plan for unexpected destroys or replacements; assess cost impact (Infracost); create change management ticket; document rollback procedure; notify team.
rule.rationale: Unexpected destroys in plan output are the most common sign of an unintended infrastructure change. A reviewed plan with no surprises is the primary safety control for production Terraform.

rule.statement: After prod apply: run health checks and smoke tests; verify monitoring alerts are active; run terraform plan again to confirm clean state (no drift).
rule.rationale: A second clean plan after apply confirms the deployed state matches configuration exactly. Drift between apply runs indicates an out-of-band change or Terraform bug.

rule.statement: Routing conclusion — preconditions are satisfied (Applies If: ALL hold, Skip If: NONE holds). Proceed to procedure / output-contract.
rule.rationale: Every methodology decision tree needs an explicit 'go' conclusion that maps back to a rule id.

rule.statement: Routing conclusion — at least one Skip-If predicate holds, or Applies-If preconditions are not all satisfied. Hand off to the named upstream / fallback methodology or stop.
rule.rationale: Explicit skip prevents partial application that produces low-confidence artefacts.

section.title: Background
section.p: Workspace limitations: share backend config, share provider configuration, not suitable for system decomposition across components, insufficient blast-radius isolation for critical production systems.
